newsitem.title: ITALY: Ex-Nazi Priebke rejects Italy court order to move.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Nazi Priebke rejects Italy court order to move.

text.p: Convicted ex-Nazi officer Erich Priebke said on Thursday he would not follow a court order to move him from an Italian hillside monastery and make him serve the rest of his jail sentence in a military hospital.

Priebke, 84, who received a five-year sentence from a Rome military court last month for his role in Italy's worst World War Two atrocity, has been living under house arrest in the Franciscan monastery since last year.
"My transferral to the military hospital is an abuse of power and I absolutely do not intend to go there," Priebke said in a letter he sent to the military court.

The Franciscan order had stipulated the former Nazi officer should leave their care after the trial ended. Priebke's lawyers had requested he be moved to the home of right-wing activist Paolo Giachini, arguing the former SS captain had no way of escaping.
The court said on Wednesday that Priebke must go to Rome's Celio hospital by August 17.

"I have indicated a home in which to serve my house arrest thus I will consider any use of force against me as a seizure and will appeal it to judicial authorities," Priebke said in the letter released by his lawyers.
"I defy any prosecutor to explain...how there is any danger I could flee."
In an interview published in Il Giornale newspaper on Thursday, Priebke had called the court's order "an attempt to clean consciences" and said he would fight it.
Priebke also told Il Giornale the move could seriously endanger his health.
"My neuro-psychiatrist is completely opposed to my moving to a hospital. He thinks this could have an irreversible impact on my health, which is already suffering."
Priebke was extradited to Italy in November, 1995, from Argentina, where he had lived openly for almost half a century, and has been held in custody ever since.
He said he desperately wanted to see his wife, who has remained in Argentina.
"After all this time I miss terribly the warmth of my family, especially my wife," Priebke said. "The only thing I really want to do before dying is to embrace her."

Priebke was sentenced to jail for participating in a 1944 massacre in which SS soldiers rounded up 335 men and boys and shot them in caves outside Rome in retaliation for a partisan attack on German occupying forces.
The conviction came at the end of a lengthy retrial after another tribunal acquitted him last August. That decision sparked outrage in Italy's Jewish community.
Priebke was immediately re-arrested and a new trial was ordered.
